title: Game Boy Color in Atomic Purple
lede: Nintendo’s colour handheld in translucent purple plastic, which shows its circuit board, speaker, and button contacts through the shell.
summary: Translucent purple shell with visible electronics and a multicolored COLOR logo. Nintendo, 1998.

creator.name: Nintendo (development team led by Satoru Okada, per Wikipedia)

made: 1998 (Japan 21 October 1998; North America 18 November 1998, per Wikipedia)

evidence.note: Inspected Evan-Amos’s 2011 photograph of one Atomic Purple unit (Commons, original 1580 × 2580; viewed at 960 × 1568) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored. The photographed unit is privately owned; no museum copy was found.

styles.note: Clear: translucent candy-colored plastic that displays the technology inside, released the same year as the iMac G3.

context: Wikipedia says the Game Boy Color launched in Japan on 21 October 1998 and in North America on 18 November 1998. “Atomic Purple”, made from translucent purple plastic, was released at the same time as the other launch colors. [Wikipedia: Game Boy Color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Color).
observed: The whole shell is translucent lilac-purple. The green circuit board, the round speaker with its copper coil, screws, and contact pads show through it.
A black glass panel frames a gray screen. Below it “GAME BOY” is in gray italic capitals and “COLOR” in red, purple, green, yellow, and blue letters.
The buttons are dark gray; the A and B buttons are round and the Select and Start buttons are pill shapes.
Every outer corner of the case is rounded.
interpretation: Translucency here is a display of the machine itself: the inner technology becomes decoration. This is a central Y2K idea, shared with the [iMac G3](ref:imac-g3-bondi-blue-1998).
Clear purple is a frequent Y2K candy color; it sits between the blues and the pinks of the palette.
borrow: Show structure through a tinted translucent surface instead of hiding it.
Use pill-shaped secondary controls next to round primary controls.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Commons photograph is released into the public domain by its author, Evan-Amos, but the product design and logos belong to Nintendo. The lead curator can decide whether the photograph may be stored (tier A) on the argument that a utilitarian product is not copyrightable.
